messages.author: bba576a74eafc909
messages.subject: Bin predictions
parts:
Hello all,

If I'm understanding correctly, the model outputs called in the Visualize/Project components are from a single run that used all the data points as training samples (no partitioning). I would like to have a model output that incorporates my selected spatial partitioning scheme (e.g., a mean/median of all bins). The individual evaluation bin statistics are provided as output, so is there anyway to get the model predictions from each bin, too?

Thanks, 
Amy

messages.author: fe049c2835236bb1
messages.subject: Bin predictions
parts:
Amy,

As I wrote in my answer to the previous question, the model objects returned in ENMeval are built from the full occurrence dataset, and the cross validation statistics are meant to help you select the optimal model settings. You cannot retrieve the models built from partitioned occurrence data in an ENMevaluation object, but you could always partition your data in R with ENMeval, run models on each subset, and use raster::predict() to make predictions.

Can I ask why you want an average of the models built from the partitioned datasets? Each of these models has less data than you started with, and theoretically the model with the most data (assuming the occurrences are accurate) should be superior to any model built with a subset. It would help if you could explain your reasoning.

Thanks,

Jamie

messages.author: bba576a74eafc909
messages.subject: Re: Bin predictions
parts:
Hi Jamie,

I'm interested in the use of the partitioning as a means of replication, to represent potential variability in the model, response curves, etc. The MaxEnt GUI does this so I assumed ENMeval did the same (which you have previously corrected for me). ENMeval has the useful benefit of non-random options (e.g., block) that the GUI does not. Though I can build the models separately and combine them myself, as you suggest, I wanted to make sure ENMeval couldn't be used to automate some of this (since it presumably makes bin-specific predictions in the background in order to get the cross validation stats?)

I work with invasive species, so value transferability. Spatially-structured model development is one way I'm attempting to mitigate the uncertainty/risk associated with that goal while using MaxEnt. Though I can understand some argument for it, a single model using all points for training seems less robust to me. If you know of a paper that offers reasoning for or against this, I'd definitely be interested.

Thanks, 
Amy

messages.author: fe049c2835236bb1
messages.subject: Re: Bin predictions
parts:
Amy,

I think I see what your intention is, but let me clarify a bit. The mean test AUC (for example) on spatially structured partitions is meant to demonstrate how well those particular model settings do, given your data, at model transfer to areas with (likely) different environmental characteristics. Summary statistics like this should help you choose which model settings are optimal for your data. Other things you may be interested in are the minimum test AUC, for example, which shows you how bad the worst model was at transfer across all partitions. The new version of ENMeval I'm working on provides these extremes by default.

However, each model made on partitioned data is inadequate by definition, in that it does not include all the available occurrences for your species. If you are trying to model your species' niche as accurately as you can manage, shouldn't you use all the data good enough to model with? The models made on partitioned data are useful for evaluation purposes, but not for estimating the species niche. Averaging them does not seem to me like a better way than using all the data. However, this model average might be useful in order to evaluate transferability in some way. If that was your intention, then I apologize for the long-winded response.

Jamie
